title: Tonga’s 2022 eruption threw a plume 57 km high, the tallest since Krakatoa in 1883
body: At 17:14 local time on 15 January 2022, the mostly underwater volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai, in the South Pacific, exploded. Its eruption column climbed to about **57 km**, punching through the stratosphere into the mesosphere, the highest recorded since Krakatoa’s in 1883. Weather satellites watched the plume burst through the clouds and spread into giant umbrella-shaped clouds. It was the largest volcanic eruption since Mount Pinatubo in 1991, and its bangs were heard in Alaska, about 9,300 km away.

cover.alt: Satellite view from above of a round grey plume with ripples, bursting up through a sheet of white cloud over the ocean

slides.alt: Satellite time-lapse looking down on the South Pacific: a dark dot appears in the clouds, swells into a rippled grey disc, and spreads into a vast pale umbrella cloud as evening darkness sweeps across.
slides.caption: 15 January 2022, seen by a GOES weather satellite: the plume punches up through the clouds and spreads out into a vast umbrella cloud as night falls.

slides.heading: How high the eruption reached
slides.note: Krakatoa’s figure is an upper estimate: its column rose “up to 80 km”

slides.prompt: People in Fiji, 700 km away, heard what sounded like thunder. What is the farthest place the bangs were reported?
slides.detail: A series of bangs was heard there at around 3:30 in the morning local time, hours after the blast.

slides.label: of seawater blasted into the stratosphere
slides.text: That was about 10% of the water vapour the stratosphere normally holds, and the excess is expected to linger for 5 to 10 years.

slides.question: Which layer of the atmosphere did the top of the plume break into?
slides.explanation: At about 57 km the column passed right through the stratosphere and broke into the mesosphere above it, the highest column on record since Krakatoa.
